title: jmpost repository guide
text: jmpost R package Bayesian joint models combine: parametric time--event (survival) submodel; linear nonlinear mixed-effects longitudinal submodel continuous marker, primarily tumour-size trajectories; one association/link terms connecting longitudinal trajectory survival. title: Covariate Selection with the Horseshoe Prior
text: Covariate selection joint models often difficult candidate covariate can interact survival model, longitudinal model, association . regularized horseshoe prior provides Bayesian shrinkage approach: include candidate covariates one model, shrink survival coefficients strongly towards zero, allow smaller number coefficients escape shrinkage supported data. jmpost, workflow available survival covariate coefficients prior_horseshoe(). vignette starts prior specification shows complete joint model example survival covariates use horseshoe prior. fitted model can inspected posterior coefficient draws shrinkage factors extracted shrinkage().

title: Covariate Selection with the Horseshoe Prior
text:
horseshoe prior global-local shrinkage prior (Carvalho, Polson, Scott 2010). global parameter shrinks coefficients towards zero, coefficient-level local parameters allow selected coefficients remain large. regularized horseshoe (Piironen Vehtari 2017) adds slab component regularizes coefficients escape main shrinkage. parameterization used jmpost, following notation brms (Bürkner 2017). Details provided statistical specifications vignette . hyperparameters map prior_horseshoe() arguments follows: df: local degrees freedom, νλ
u_{\lambda} df_global: global degrees freedom, ντ
u_{	au} df_slab: slab degrees freedom, νc
u_c scale_global: global scale, sτs_{	au} scale_slab: slab scale, scs_c local shrinkage parameters λj\lambda_j let individual coefficients escape global shrinkage τ	au. slab scale scs_c slab degrees freedom νc
u_c control much large coefficients regularized. Smaller sτs_{	au} values encode stronger prior belief small number candidate covariates relevant. useful posterior diagnostic shrinkage factor κj=11+τ2λj2/c2. \kappa_j =  rac{1}{1 + 	au^2\lambda_j^2 / c^2}. Values κj\kappa_j close 1 indicate strong shrinkage towards zero. Values close 0 indicate little shrinkage. shrinkage factor read together coefficient posterior: evidence strongly prior-likelihood combination pulled coefficient towards zero, standalone posterior inclusion probability.

code: set.seed(129) sim_data <- SimJointData(     design = list(         SimGroup(50, "Arm-A", "Study-X"),         SimGroup(50, "Arm-B", "Study-X")     ),     longitudinal = SimLongitudinalRandomSlope(         times = c(1, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300),         intercept = 30,         slope_mu = c(1, 2),         slope_sigma = 0.2,         sigma = 20,         link_dsld = 0.1     ),     survival = SimSurvivalWeibullPH(         lambda = 1 / 300,         gamma = 0.97,         time_max = 2000,         time_step = 1,         lambda_cen = 1 / 9000,         beta_cat = c(             "A" = 0,             "B" = 0.3,             "C" = 0.7         ),         beta_cont = 0.3     ) ) os_data <- sim_data@survival long_data <- sim_data@longitudinal  joint_data <- DataJoint(     subject = DataSubject(         data = os_data,         subject = "subject",         arm = "arm",         study = "study"     ),     survival = DataSurvival(         data = os_data,         formula = Surv(time, event) ~ cov_cat + cov_cont     ),     longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(         data = long_data,         formula = sld ~ time,         threshold = 5     ) ) head(model.matrix(joint_data@survival)) #>      cov_catB cov_catC   cov_cont #> [1,]        1        0 -1.1209000 #> [2,]        0        1 -0.9897245 #> [3,]        0        1 -1.3746970 #> [4,]        0        1 -1.3556451 #> [5,]        1        0  1.9967553 #> [6,]        1        0  0.6958700 survival_covariates <- covariates(joint_data@survival) survival_covariates #> [1] "cov_catB" "cov_catC" "cov_cont"

title: Covariate Selection with the Horseshoe Prior
text: Now define joint model. longitudinal model association link use standard priors. survival model uses prior_horseshoe() vector survival covariate coefficients: choice uses half-Cauchy priors local global shrinkage parameters, df = 1 df_global = 1. relatively small scale_global = 0.3 favours sparse survival effects small example, scale_slab = 2 still allows meaningfully large log-hazard coefficients data support . following code fits model. serious analysis, increase number warmup sampling iterations check convergence carefully.
code: joint_model <- JointModel(     longitudinal = LongitudinalRandomSlope(),     survival = SurvivalWeibullPH(         beta = prior_horseshoe(             df = 1,             df_global = 1,             df_slab = 4,             scale_global = 0.3,             scale_slab = 2         )     ),     link = linkDSLD() ) fit <- sampleStanModel(     joint_model,     data = joint_data,     iter_warmup = 500,     iter_sampling = 500,     chains = 4,     parallel_chains = 4,     seed = 325,     refresh = 0,     show_exceptions = FALSE,     show_messages = FALSE ) #> Warning: 7 of 2000 (0.0%) transitions ended with a divergence. #> See https://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings for details.

title: Fitting a Custom Longitudinal Model with Covariates
text: vignette gives complete implementation custom longitudinal model whose population parameters depend subject-level covariates. extends Wang, Sung et al. (2009) mixed exponential-decay linear-growth example custom longitudinal model vignette. general extension interfaces described Extending jmpost. use longitudinal model yi(t)∼N(bie−sit+git,σ2),bi∼LogNormal⁡(ηb,,ωb),si∼LogNormal⁡(log(μs),ωs),gi∼LogNormal⁡(ηg,,ωg),ηb,=βb,0+Xb,iβb,ηg,=βg,0+Xg,iβg. \begin{align} y_i(t) &\sim N\left(b_i e^{-s_i t} + g_i t,\ \sigma^2\right), \\ b_i &\sim \operatorname{LogNormal}\left(\eta_{b,},\ \omega_b\right), \\ s_i &\sim \operatorname{LogNormal}\left(\log(\mu_s),\ \omega_s\right), \\ g_i &\sim \operatorname{LogNormal}\left(\eta_{g,},\ \omega_g\right), \\ \eta_{b,} &= \beta_{b,0} + X_{b,}\beta_b, \\ \eta_{g,} &= \beta_{g,0} + X_{g,}\beta_g. \end{align} , Xb,iX_{b,} Xg,iX_{g,} independently specified design-matrix rows. Consequently, baseline growth distributions can use different covariates. intercepts coefficients log scale, population medians bib_i gig_i positive. survival submodel derivative link example without longitudinal covariates: log⁡hi(t)=log⁡(λ0)+α{−sibie−sit+gi}. \log h_i(t) = \log(\lambda_0) + \alpha\left\{-s_i b_i e^{-s_i t} + g_i\right\}. example deliberately implements covariate handling . real application, course first check whether one jmpost’s built-covariate models already describes required trajectory.

code: SimWangCov <- setClass(     "SimWangCov",     contains = "SimLongitudinal",     slots = c(         times = "numeric",         mu_baseline = "numeric",         baseline_arm_ratio = "numeric",         mu_shrinkage = "numeric",         mu_growth = "numeric",         growth_arm_ratio = "numeric",         omega_baseline = "numeric",         omega_shrinkage = "numeric",         omega_growth = "numeric",         sigma = "numeric",         link_dsld = "numeric"     ) )  sampleSubjects.SimWangCov <- function(object, subjects_df) {     arm_b <- as.numeric(subjects_df$arm == "Arm-B")     n_subjects <- nrow(subjects_df)      subjects_df$baseline <- rlnorm(         n_subjects,         log(object@mu_baseline) + log(object@baseline_arm_ratio) * arm_b,         object@omega_baseline     )     subjects_df$shrinkage <- rlnorm(         n_subjects,         log(object@mu_shrinkage),         object@omega_shrinkage     )     subjects_df$growth <- rlnorm(         n_subjects,         log(object@mu_growth) + log(object@growth_arm_ratio) * arm_b,         object@omega_growth     )     subjects_df }  sampleObservations.SimWangCov <- function(object, times_df) {     expected <- with(         times_df,         baseline * exp(-shrinkage * time) + growth * time     )     derivative <- with(         times_df,         growth - baseline * shrinkage * exp(-shrinkage * time)     )      times_df$sld <- rnorm(nrow(times_df), expected, object@sigma)     times_df$log_haz_link <- object@link_dsld * derivative     times_df }  set.seed(7294) simulated <- SimJointData(     design = list(         SimGroup(25, "Arm-A", "Study-X"),         SimGroup(25, "Arm-B", "Study-X")     ),     survival = SimSurvivalExponential(         lambda = 365 / 500,         time_max = 3,         time_step = 1 / 365,         lambda_censor = 1 / 30     ),     longitudinal = SimWangCov(         times = c(1, 60, 120, 240, 400, 650, 900) / 365,         mu_baseline = 60,         baseline_arm_ratio = 1.25,         mu_shrinkage = 2,         mu_growth = 10,         growth_arm_ratio = 1.4,         omega_baseline = 0.25,         omega_shrinkage = 0.25,         omega_growth = 0.25,         sigma = 1.5,         link_dsld = 0.02     ),     .silent = TRUE )  dat_lm <- simulated@longitudinal dat_os <- simulated@survival  dat_lm |>     filter(subject %in% head(unique(subject), 8)) |>     ggplot(aes(time, sld, group = subject, colour = arm)) +     geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +     geom_point() +     labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Tumour size", colour = "Arm") +     theme_bw()

text: DataLongitudinal() deliberately continues use outcome ~ time formula. Longitudinal covariates subject-level variables belong data passed DataSubject(). longitudinal_model_stan_data.<class>() method turns variables model-specific Stan data. helper removes usual intercept column Stan model explicit intercept parameters. reference argument preserves fitted factor levels, contrasts, column order formula applied new population profiles. method name must end exact S4 class name. jmpost calls converting DataJoint Stan data, users need construct append matrices .
code: covariate_design <- function(formula, data, reference = data) {     reference_frame <- model.frame(         formula,         data = reference,         na.action = na.fail     )     formula_terms <- terms(reference_frame)     reference_design <- model.matrix(formula_terms, reference_frame)      data_frame <- model.frame(         formula_terms,         data = data,         xlev = stats::.getXlevels(formula_terms, reference_frame),         na.action = na.fail     )     design <- model.matrix(         formula_terms,         data_frame,         contrasts.arg = attr(reference_design, "contrasts")     )     design[, colnames(design) != "(Intercept)", drop = FALSE] }  longitudinal_model_stan_data.WangCovModel <- function(model, subject) {     subject_data <- as.data.frame(subject)     baseline_design <- covariate_design(         model@baseline_formula,         subject_data     )     growth_design <- covariate_design(         model@growth_formula,         subject_data     )      list(         p_baseline_cov = ncol(baseline_design),         baseline_cov_design = baseline_design,         p_growth_cov = ncol(growth_design),         growth_cov_design = growth_design     ) }

code: enableLink.WangCovModel <- function(object, ...) {     object@stan <- merge(         object@stan,         StanModule("custom-cov-model-enable-link.stan")     )     object }  link <- LinkComponent(     stan = StanModule("custom-cov-model-dsld.stan"),     prior = prior_normal(0, 0.5),     key = "link_dsld" ) transformed parameters {     matrix[n_subjects, 3] link_function_inputs;     link_function_inputs[, 1] = baseline_idv;     link_function_inputs[, 2] = shrinkage_idv;     link_function_inputs[, 3] = growth_idv; } functions {     matrix link_dsld_contrib(matrix time, matrix link_function_inputs) {         int nrow = rows(time);         int ncol = cols(time);         matrix[nrow, ncol] baseline = rep_matrix(link_function_inputs[, 1], ncol);         matrix[nrow, ncol] shrinkage = rep_matrix(link_function_inputs[, 2], ncol);         matrix[nrow, ncol] growth = rep_matrix(link_function_inputs[, 3], ncol);         return growth - baseline .* shrinkage .* exp(-shrinkage .* time);     } }

title: Fitting a Custom Longitudinal Model
text: vignette shows complete example fit custom longitudinal model. Note full details various different interfaces can found “Extending jmpost” vignette. example implements Wang, Sung et al. 2009 mixed exponential decay linear growth model along exponential survival model. particular following model implemented: Longitudinal Model: yi(t)∼N(μi(t),σ2)μi(t)=bie−sit+gitbi∼LogNormal(μb,σb)si∼LogNormal(μs,σs)gi∼LogNormal(μg,σg) \begin{align} y_{}(t) &\sim N\left(\mu_i(t),\ \sigma^2\right) \\ \\ \mu_i(t) &= b_i e^{-s_it} + g_i t  \\ \\ b_i &\sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_b,\ \sigma_b) \\ s_i &\sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_s,\ \sigma_s) \\ g_i &\sim \text{LogNormal}(\mu_g,\ \sigma_g) \\ \end{align} : * ii subject index * yi(t)y_{}(t) observed tumour size measurement subject ii time tt * μi(t)\mu_i(t) expected tumour size measurement subject ii time tt * bib_i subject baseline tumour size measurement * sis_i subject kinetics shrinkage parameter * gig_i subject kinetics tumour growth parameter * μθ\mu_{\theta} population mean parameter θ\theta * ωθ\omega_{\theta} population standard deviation parameter θ\theta. Survival Model: log⁡(hi(t))=log⁡(λ0)+Xiβ+G(t∣bi,si,gi) \log(h_i(t)) = \log(\lambda_0) + X_i \beta + G(t \mid b_i, s_i, g_i) : λ0\lambda_0 baseline hazard rate. example using exponential survival model e.g. h0(t)=λ0h_0(t) = \lambda_0 tt event time G(.)G(.) link function maps subjects tumour growth parameters contribution log-hazard function XiX_i subjects covariate design matrix β\beta corresponding coefficients vector scale design matrix covariates contribution log-hazard function example just consider derivative growth function link function, e.g. G(t∣bi,si,gi)=−sibie−sit+gi G(t \mid b_i, s_i, g_i) = -s_i b_i e^{-s_i t} + g_i keep example simple, number features implemented package’s internal models skipped; may wish consider adding implementing model real project. particular following omitted example: Handling censored observations (e.g. observations limit quantification) Separate populations per study / arm Non-centred parameterisation hierarchical parameters (parameterisation leads better performance small numbers observations per subject). code: # Define our simulation parameters + object SimWang <- setClass(     "SimWang",     contains = "SimLongitudinal",     slots = c(         times = "numeric",         mu_b = "numeric",         mu_s = "numeric",         mu_g = "numeric",         omega_b = "numeric",         omega_s = "numeric",         omega_g = "numeric",         sigma = "numeric",         link_dsld = "numeric"     ) )  # Method to generate individual subjects parameters from the hierarchical distributions sampleSubjects.SimWang <- function(object, subjects_df) {     nsub <- nrow(subjects_df)     subjects_df$b <- stats::rlnorm(nsub, log(object@mu_b), object@omega_b)     subjects_df$s <- stats::rlnorm(nsub, log(object@mu_s), object@omega_s)     subjects_df$g <- stats::rlnorm(nsub, log(object@mu_g), object@omega_g)     subjects_df }  # Method to generate observations for each individual subject sampleObservations.SimWang <- function(object, times_df) {     nobs <- nrow(times_df)     calc_mu <- function(time, b, s, g) b * exp(-s * time) + g * time     calc_dsld <- function(time, b, s, g) -s * b * exp(-s * time) + g      times_df$mu_sld <- calc_mu(times_df$time, times_df$b, times_df$s, times_df$g)     times_df$dsld <- calc_dsld(times_df$time, times_df$b, times_df$s, times_df$g)     times_df$sld <- stats::rnorm(nobs, times_df$mu_sld, object@sigma)     times_df$log_haz_link <- object@link_dsld * times_df$dsld     times_df }   # Generate simulated data set.seed(1622) joint_data_sim <- SimJointData(     design = list(SimGroup(80, "Arm-A", "Study-X")),     survival = SimSurvivalExponential(         lambda = (1 / 400) * 365,         time_max = 4,         time_step = 1 / 365,         lambda_censor = 1 / 9000,         beta_cat = c("A" = 0, "B" = -0.1, "C" = 0.5),         beta_cont = 0.3     ),     longitudinal = SimWang(         times = c(             1, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 600,             800, 1000, 1300, 1600         ) / 365,         mu_b = 60,         mu_s = 2,         mu_g = 10,         omega_b = 0.3,         omega_s = 0.3,         omega_g = 0.3,         sigma = 1.5,         link_dsld = 0.2     ),     .silent = TRUE )  dat_lm <- joint_data_sim@longitudinal dat_os <- joint_data_sim@survival   # Select 6 random subjects to plot dat_lm_plot <- dat_lm |>     filter(subject %in% sample(dat_os$subject, 6))  ggplot(dat_lm_plot, aes(x = time, y = sld, group = subject, color = subject)) +     geom_line() +     geom_point() +     labs(x = "Time (years)", y = "Tumour Size", col = "Subject") +     theme_bw() +     theme(legend.position = "bottom")

we want jmpost to generate             # initial values automatically for us             Parameter(                 name = "baseline_idv",                 prior = set_limits(                     prior_init_only(prior_lognormal(log(60), 1)),                     lower = getOption("jmpost.double_eps")                 ),                 size = "n_subjects"             ),             Parameter( functions {     // Expected tumour size value     vector sld(vector tumour_time, vector baseline, vector shrinkage, vector growth) {         vector[rows(tumour_time)] tumour_value;         tumour_value = baseline .* exp(- shrinkage .* tumour_time)  +                        growth .* tumour_time;         return tumour_value;     } }  transformed parameters{      // Calculated the fitted Tumour values     vector[n_tumour_all] Ypred = sld(         tumour_time,         baseline_idv[subject_tumour_index],         shrinkage_idv[subject_tumour_index],         growth_idv[subject_tumour_index]     );      // Calculate per observation log-likelihood for {loo} integration     // These values are automatically added to the target for you     long_obvs_log_lik = vect_normal_log_dens(         tumour_value,         Ypred,         rep_vector(sigma, n_tumour_all) // broadcast sigma to the length of Ypred     ); }  model {     // Define the heirarchical relationship between the individual     // and population level parameters     baseline_idv ~ lognormal(log(mu_baseline), sigma_baseline);     shrinkage_idv ~ lognormal(log(mu_shrinkage), sigma_shrinkage);     growth_idv ~ lognormal(log(mu_growth), sigma_growth); }

title: Extending jmpost
text: Survival distributions jmpost specified via contribution log-hazard function. Survival distributions implemented S4 classes inherit SurvivalModel. two main components SurvivalModel object stan parameters slots. parameters slot ParameterList() object used declare parameter used survival distribution specify prior distribution, well declare design matrix coefficients (please see “Prior Specification” section ). stan slot StanModule() object needs define following: transformed parameters block must define vector called pars_os contains one element parameter used survival distribution. functions block must define function called log_h0 returns log-hazard contribution. function must following signature: : - return matrix must dimensionality time argument matrix element log-hazard contribution corresponding timepoint time matrix. - time matrix contains one row per unique subject one column per timepoint subject - pars_os vector defined (1) contains parameters particular distribution. example following roughly equivalent Weibull distribution implemented:

title: Analyzing the PRIME Study Data
text: vignette prepares data PRIME study (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00364013) analysis jmpost. PRIME randomised, multicentre, phase III study previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer. compared first-line FOLFOX alone FOLFOX plus panitumumab: 1,183 participants randomised, 590 comparator arm 593 panitumumab arm. study’s primary aim assess whether adding panitumumab improved progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival, response, duration response, time progression, safety assessed secondary outcomes. study completed August 2009.

title: Analyzing the PRIME Study Data
text: fortunate access PRIME study data via Project Data Sphere (RRID:SCR_003726) (Green et al. 2015). supplied data ADaM-format SAS datasets. begin subject-level dataset (adsl) obtain participant’s treatment assignment survival PFS outcome. Longitudinal tumour measurements taken lesion dataset (adls): VISITDY provides analysis time LSSLD sum longest diameters used tumour-size marker. retain participant identifier (SUBJID) datasets subject-level event information can joined repeated measurements. biomarker (biomark) dataset contains KRAS mutation status participant. First read datasets supplied zip file, using simple helper function: Next create analysis datasets: want use baseline covariates analysis, need make sure discarded patients missing baseline covariates. end two analysis datasets: event_df 428 rows contains subject-level information including survival (EVENTYR time event years, EVENTFL event indicator 1 indicating patient died 0 time censored), biom_df 2474 rows contains longitudinal tumour measurements (BIOMYR time years BIOMVAL sum longest diameters millimeters). filtered certain observations subject IDs 000424, 000442, 000710. SUBJID variable serves unique identifier participant across datasets. also center scale two continuous covariates, age baseline SLD: important coefficients scale thus help prior setting convergence MCMC sampling.

title: Analyzing the PRIME Study Data
text: Now let’s continue joint model analysis using jmpost package. use covariates overall survival well growth shrinkage means: First create DataJoint object combines subject-level longitudinal data, specifying appropriate formulas longitudinal survival components: Next specify joint model including covariates now longitudinal component: can run MCMC sampler: start small HMC step size reduce numerical underflow early proposals. Stan continues adapt step size warmup. settings establish 100 warmup iterations sufficient final analysis. Let’s check convergence MCMC chains population level parameters: see sampling worked ok, R-hat values around 1. also confirmed looking trace plots: plot chunk unnamed-chunk-4 can now inspect covariate coefficients overall survival (OS), tumour growth tumour shrinkage. covariate-selection vignette, coef() uses fitted design-matrix column names label posterior summaries automatically. growth shrinkage models use covariate formula . table reports posterior medians 90% credible intervals (q5 q95), alongside R-hat bulk effective sample size. OS coefficients log-hazard scale: exponentiating coefficient gives hazard ratio, conditional covariates linked tumour trajectory. growth shrinkage coefficients act log scale respective rates, exponentiating gives ratio population median rates. Positive coefficients therefore indicate higher mortality hazard, faster growth faster shrinkage, respectively. age baseline SLD, coefficient describes one-standard-deviation increase; factor coefficients compare named level reference level. Intervals span zero indicate uncertainty direction association. can also try use horseshoe priors order variable selection: use partial non-centring horseshoe coefficients centre subject-specific growth shrinkage effects. choices change sampling coordinates preserving prior distributions likelihood. scale_noncentred argument computational tuning parameter, separate global shrinkage slab scales. Note longer warmup sampling run alone resolve divergent transitions persistent treedepth saturation. can run MCMC sampler: Let’s check convergence: assess convergence using sampler diagnostics . see across 4 chains single divergent transition, none reached maximum treedepth E-BFMI (Energy Bayesian Fraction Missing Information) values 0.5, already values 0.3 indicate good exploration posterior. Let’s check traceplots: plot chunk unnamed-chunk-6 look good, . Let’s look shrinkage factors: Let’s tabulate variable, median 5% 95% quantiles: see covariates high shrinkage values close 1, indicates covariate important outcome used model. Exceptions 95% quantile 1 following: longitudinal.mu_s:LIVERMETY: liver metastases shrinkage longitudinal.mu_g:BASE_SLD: baseline SLD growth ECOG_BIN1+: ECOG 1+/0 survival hazard can compare coefficient estimates: Also see 95% credible interval excludes 0 covariates seen shrinkage factors 1: ECOG_BIN1+ survival LIVERMETY shrinkage BASE_SLD growth Interestingly also see addition AGE survival ECOG_BIN1+ growth (Indeed use 4 digits rounding upper quantile can also see already.)
code: cov_form <- ~ ATRT + AGE + SEX + ECOG_BIN + KRAS + LIVERMET + PRIMARY_SITE + BASE_SLD library(jmpost)  jm_dat <- DataJoint(   subject = DataSubject(     data = event_df,     subject = "SUBJID",     arm = "ATRT",     study = "STUDY"   ),   longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(     data = biom_df,     threshold = 3,     formula = BIOMVAL ~ BIOMYR   ),   survival = DataSurvival(     data = event_df,     formula = update(cov_form, Surv(EVENTYR, EVENTFL) ~ .)   ) ) #> Error: #> ! There are subjects in `longitudinal` that are not present in `subjects` jm_spec <- JointModel(   longitudinal = LongitudinalSteinFojoCov(     # Baseline - there is only one study here so just intercept:     mu_b_formula = ~1,     omega_b_formula = ~1,     # Shrinkage - include covariates for the mean:     mu_s_formula = cov_form,     omega_s_formula = ~1,     # Growth - include covariates for the mean:     mu_g_formula = cov_form,     omega_g_formula = ~1,     # Baseline intercept priors:     mu_b_intercept_prior = prior_normal(4.09434, 1),     omega_b_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.60944, 1),     # Shrinkage priors:     mu_s_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-0.69315, 1),     mu_s_coefficients_prior = prior_normal(0, 1),     omega_s_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.60944, 1),     # Growth priors:     mu_g_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.20397, 1),     mu_g_coefficients_prior = prior_normal(0, 1),     omega_g_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.60944, 1),     sigma = prior_lognormal(log(10), 1)   ),   survival = SurvivalWeibullPH(beta = prior_normal(0, 1)),   # For a 10 mm/year difference, this puts approximately 95% prior probability on hazard ratios between 0.38 and 2.66:   link = linkDSLD(prior = prior_normal(0, 0.05)) ) jm_samples_file <- "samples/jm_samples_clean.rds" if (file.exists(jm_samples_file)) {   jm_samples <- readRDS(jm_samples_file) } else {   options("jmpost.prior_shrinkage" = 0.999)   set.seed(12345) # Reproduce the initial values generated in R.   jm_samples <- sampleStanModel(     jm_spec,     data = jm_dat,     iter_warmup = 1000,     iter_sampling = 1000,     # smaller starting step eliminated the gamma/lognormal exceptions:     step_size = 0.001,     chains = 4,     parallel_chains = 4,     seed = 12345   )   saveObject(jm_samples, file = jm_samples_file) } pop_pars <- c(   "lm_sfc_mu_b_intercept",   "lm_sfc_mu_g_intercept",   "lm_sfc_mu_g_coefficients",   "lm_sfc_mu_s_intercept",   "lm_sfc_mu_s_coefficients",   "lm_sfc_omega_b_intercept",   "lm_sfc_omega_g_intercept",   "lm_sfc_omega_s_intercept",   "lm_sfc_sigma",   "sm_weibull_ph_gamma",   "sm_weibull_ph_lambda",   "beta_os_cov",   "link_coefficients" )  jm_mcmc <- cmdstanr::as.CmdStanMCMC(jm_samples) jm_summary <- jm_mcmc$summary(pop_pars) summary(jm_summary$rhat) #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.  #>   1.000   1.001   1.002   1.005   1.007   1.024 jm_draws <- jm_mcmc$draws(pop_pars)  library(bayesplot) mcmc_trace(jm_draws) coefficient_summary <- coef(jm_samples) |>   dplyr::mutate(     component = dplyr::case_when(       component == "survival" ~ "OS",       predictor == "mu_g" ~ "Growth",       predictor == "mu_s" ~ "Shrinkage"     )   ) |>   dplyr::select(component, covariate, median, q5, q95, rhat, ess_bulk) knitr::kable(coefficient_summary, digits = 3) jm_horseshoe_spec <- JointModel(   longitudinal = LongitudinalSteinFojoCov(     # Baseline - there is only one study here so just intercept:     mu_b_formula = ~1,     omega_b_formula = ~1,     # Shrinkage - include covariates for the mean:     mu_s_formula = cov_form,     omega_s_formula = ~1,     # Growth - include covariates for the mean:     mu_g_formula = cov_form,     omega_g_formula = ~1,     # Baseline intercept priors:     mu_b_intercept_prior = prior_normal(4.09434, 1),     omega_b_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.60944, 1),     # Shrinkage priors:     mu_s_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-0.69315, 1),     mu_s_coefficients_prior = prior_horseshoe(scale_noncentred = 0.1),     omega_s_intercept_prior = prior_normal(-1.60944, 1),     # title: jmpost Quickstart
text: JointModel needs specified three parts: longitudinal: model longitudinal outcomes. survival: model survival outcomes. link: link specifies longitudinal model parameters enter survival model. FALSE    #> 6 subject_001 Arm-A Study-X   200 271.  FALSE joint_data <- DataJoint(     subject = DataSubject(         data = os_data,         subject = "subject",         arm = "arm",         study = "study"     ),     survival = DataSurvival(         data = os_data,         formula = Surv(time, event) ~ cov_cat + cov_cont     ),     longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(         data = long_data,         formula = sld ~ time,         threshold = 5     ) ) head(model.matrix(joint_data@survival)) #>      cov_catB cov_catC   cov_cont #> [1,]        1        0 -1.1209000 #> [2,]        0        1 -0.9897245 #> [3,]        0        1 -1.3746970 #> [4,]        0        1 -1.3556451 #> [5,]        1        0  1.9967553 #> [6,]        1        0  0.6958700

title: jmpost Quickstart
text: covariate longitudinal models allow subject-level baseline covariates affect parameters longitudinal trajectory. provided LongitudinalRandomSlopeCov(), LongitudinalSteinFojoCov(), LongitudinalGSFCov(), LongitudinalClaretBrunoCov(). constructor uses one-sided formulas specify covariates model parameter. variables formulas must columns data passed DataSubject(). intercept column implied formula removed predictor separate *_intercept_prior; corresponding *_coefficients_prior controls remaining design-matrix coefficients. example, ~ arm + cov_cont models differences reference arm together linear effect cov_cont. Predictors can use "linear", "proportional", "exponential", "log-linear" parametrizations. defaults use linear predictors location parameters log-linear predictors scale parameters, keeping latter positive. Covariates may differ parameters may overlap , differ , covariates survival model. following short example uses data prepared . lets continuous baseline covariate affect subject intercept, treatment arm affect mean slope, uses common slope standard deviation. usual DataJoint() sampleStanModel() workflow otherwise unchanged. coefficient names order follow non-intercept columns formula’s design matrix. real analysis, use informative priors possible, run longer chains, assess convergence described .
code: covariate_model <- JointModel(     longitudinal = LongitudinalRandomSlopeCov(         mu_formula = ~cov_cont,         slope_mu_formula = ~arm,         slope_sigma_formula = ~1,         mu_intercept_prior = prior_normal(30, 10),         mu_coefficients_prior = prior_normal(0, 3),         slope_mu_intercept_prior = prior_normal(1, 2),         slope_mu_coefficients_prior = prior_normal(0, 2),         slope_sigma_intercept_prior = prior_normal(log(0.2), 0.5),         sigma = prior_lognormal(log(20), 0.5)     ) )  set.seed(481) covariate_results <- sampleStanModel(     covariate_model,     data = joint_data,     iter_sampling = 100,     iter_warmup = 100,     chains = 1,     parallel_chains = 1,     refresh = 0 ) #> Running MCMC with 1 chain... #>  #> Chain 1 WARNING: There aren't enough warmup iterations to fit the  #> Chain 1          three stages of adaptation as currently configured.  #> Chain 1          Reducing each adaptation stage to 15%/75%/10% of  #> Chain 1          the given number of warmup iterations:  #> Chain 1            init_buffer = 15  #> Chain 1            adapt_window = 75  #> Chain 1            term_buffer = 10  #> Chain 1 finished in 0.2 seconds.  cmdstanr::as.CmdStanMCMC(covariate_results)$summary(     c(         "lm_rsc_mu_intercept",         "lm_rsc_mu_coefficients",         "lm_rsc_slope_mu_intercept",         "lm_rsc_slope_mu_coefficients"     ) ) #> Warning: The ESS has been capped to avoid unstable estimates. #> # A tibble: 4 × 10 #>   variable        mean median     sd    mad     q5   q95  rhat ess_bulk ess_tail #>   <chr>          <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl> #> 1 lm_rsc_mu_in… 27.6   27.6   0.486  0.554  26.7   28.3  1.28      2.83     16.6 #> 2 lm_rsc_mu_co…  1.80   1.80  0.329  0.379   1.24   2.27 1.41      2.28     21.0 #> 3 lm_rsc_slope…  1.02   1.02  0.0363 0.0395  0.963  1.07 1.01    133.       59.9 #> 4 lm_rsc_slope…  0.949  0.954 0.0560 0.0531  0.856  1.03 0.993   200       102.

code: os_data <- sim_data_end@survival long_data <- sim_data_end@longitudinal joint_data <- DataJoint(     subject = DataSubject(         data = os_data,         subject = "subject",         arm = "arm",         study = "study"     ),     survival = DataSurvival(         data = os_data,         formula = Surv(time, event) ~ cov_cat + cov_cont     ),     longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(         data = long_data,         formula = sld ~ time,         threshold = 5     ) )   sf_model <- JointModel(     longitudinal = LongitudinalSteinFojo(         mu_bsld = prior_normal(log(60), 0.2),         mu_ks = prior_normal(-3, 0.4),         mu_kg = prior_normal(log(0.005), 0.3),         centred = TRUE     ),     survival = SurvivalWeibullPH(),     link = linkDSLD() ) set.seed(202671) mcmc_results <- sampleStanModel(     sf_model,     data = joint_data,     iter_sampling = 1000,     iter_warmup = 500,     chains = 4,     parallel_chains = 4,     step_size = 0.01 ) knitr::kable(     mcmc_results@results$summary(         c("lm_sf_mu_bsld", "lm_sf_mu_ks", "lm_sf_mu_kg", "lm_sf_omega_bsld", "lm_sf_omega_ks", "lm_sf_omega_ks")     ),     digits = 3 )

title: Joint Models for Predicting Overall Survival Trajectories
text: goal jmpost package fit joint models involving: parametric time--event sub-model, nonlinear (linear) mixed-effect sub-model, describing individual time profiles (.e. trajectories) continuous marker, link function (.k.. association term). specifically, model implemented package utilizes modelling framework described previously [1-3] link overall survival tumour size data oncology clinical trials. [1] Tardivon et al. Association tumour size kinetics survival patients urothelial carcinoma treated atezolizumab: Implications patient follow-. Clin Pharm Ther, 2019.[2] Kerioui et al. Bayesian inference using Hamiltonian Monte-Carlo algorithm nonlinear joint modelling context cancer immunotherapy. Stat Med, 2020.[3] Kerioui et al. Modelling association biomarkers clinical outcome: introduction nonlinear joint models. Br J Clin Pharm, 2022. models implemented STAN, package provides flexible user interface. Please reach us via issues email (see DESCRIPTION file) comments questions like get involved ongoing development, thank !

title: Joint Models for Predicting Overall Survival Trajectories
text: See also model fitting vignette details. present basic example . First simulate data set. practice want follow similar structure input data use DataJoint() bring right format. specify joint model, use Generalized Stein-Fojo model longitudinal part, Weibull proportional hazards model survival part. longitudinal model impacts hazard via term derivative another term time--growth. Finally can sample parameters via MCMC underlying Stan model. Note real application choose warm sampling iterations.
code: library(jmpost) #> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggpp': #>   method                  from    #>   heightDetails.titleGrob ggplot2 #>   widthDetails.titleGrob  ggplot2 set.seed(321) sim_data <- SimJointData(     design = list(         SimGroup(50, "Arm-A", "Study-X"),         SimGroup(50, "Arm-B", "Study-X")     ),     longitudinal = SimLongitudinalRandomSlope(         times = c(1, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300),     ),     survival = SimSurvivalWeibullPH(         lambda = 1 / 300,         gamma = 0.97     ) ) #> INFO: 1 subject(s) did not die before max(times)  joint_data <- DataJoint(     subject = DataSubject(         data = sim_data@survival,         subject = "subject",         arm = "arm",         study = "study"     ),     survival = DataSurvival(         data = sim_data@survival,         formula = Surv(time, event) ~ cov_cat + cov_cont     ),     longitudinal = DataLongitudinal(         data = sim_data@longitudinal,         formula = sld ~ time,         threshold = 5     ) ) joint_model <- JointModel(     longitudinal = LongitudinalGSF(),     survival = SurvivalWeibullPH(),     link = Link(         linkDSLD(),         linkTTG()     ) ) mcmc_results <- sampleStanModel(     joint_model,     data = joint_data,     iter_sampling = 100,     iter_warmup = 100,     chains = 1,     parallel_chains = 1 )

title: jmpost (development version)
text: Added prior_flat() constant prior density model parameter scale, configurable distribution used initial values. Added package-defined exponential positive-branch square prior transformations transform scalar prior helpers prior_transform(), automatic Jacobians, mapped truncation bounds initial values. Updated quickstart, statistical specification, extension guide. Added longitudinal models supporting covariate modeling: LongitudinalRandomSlopeCov, LongitudinalSteinFojoCov, LongitudinalGSFCov LongitudinalClaretBrunoCov classes implement corresponding covariate versions already existing longitudinal models. Please see quick start vignette short introduction. also possible add new custom longitudinal models covariates; new vignette added describe required components. LongitudinalModel objects now new slot scaled_variance stores used variance option, part print output now thereby transparently communicating user choice multiplicative additive error model. Changed default longitudinal model option scaled_variance FALSE, corresponding additive error model (simulation well inference functions). Also added option random effects model consistency models. Included new populationHR() function calculate population effects JointModelSample object, marginalising patient-level random effects (#447). Included new LongitudinalRandomEffects() function can used extract patient-level random effects parameter samples JointModelSample object (#423). Introduced saveObject() method JointModelSample objects order serialise disk (#431). Added support truncated prior distributions e.g. can now apply normal prior strictly positive parameter jmpost take care adjusting density accordingly (#429). Added prior_normal_vector() can used assign different normal prior distributions coefficients survival model covariates. Added prior_const() prior_const_vector() fixes parameter (vector) constant value, .e. uses point-mass prior distribution. Added prior_horseshoe() uses horseshoe prior components parameter vector, typically coefficients survival model covariates. Stan files associated models longer hardcode parameter declarations. task now handled Prior objects. constant value used parameter instead prior distribution, parameter declared data block reassigned transformed_parameters block. Included new Gamma distribution survival model (#411). Reworked LOO calculations apply individual submodel disabled LOO calculations overall joint model (#402). Added support additive variance (#403). Added support independent variances per study/arm (#389). Miscellaneous bug fixes. Introduce new package options bounds close zero used avoid MCMC sampler starting warnings.
